newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-P.Lehman sees strong 96/97 Q1 growth.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-P.Lehman sees strong 96/97 Q1 growth.

text.p: Premium wine producer Peter Lehmann Wines Ltd said on Friday that 1996/97 unaudited first quarter results showed continuing substantial growth on the same period last year.

"I am pleased to report that the 1996/97 (July-June) unaudited first quarter results show continuing substantial growth over the same quarter last year," chairman Des Ross told the company's annual meeting.
"I know of no factor which would impact upon a good half yearly result but, as always, the second half result will be influenced by the weather and resulting vintage," he said.

Chief executive officer Doug Lehmann told shareholders that revenue from domestic sales rose over the previous year's first quarter with the company gaining increased distribution in a very competitive market.
Export sales for the first quarter had been very buoyant with growth in revenue and volume exceeding the corresponding period of the previous year, he said.
"The company's major export markets, namely the United Kingdom, United States and New Zealand, have all experienced significant growth during this period," he said.
"The much smaller markets of Asia and Europe have maintained acceptable sales levels," he said.
Peter Lehmann reported a 39 percent rise in net profit to A$1.8 million for 1995/96.

Lehmann said climatic conditions through winter and spring had been excellent, and, despite some small isolated pockets of frost experienced in September, the outlook at this stage for the 1997 vintage looked very promising.
To continue to improve efficiencies, further capital expansion of A$1.03 million was planned for 1996/97, to be financed through bank borrowings, he said.

Ross said the company would need increasing quantities of quality fruit if it was to continue appropriate growth, and this would be procured from existing growers who engage in a vine replanting programme as well as from new sources.
Growers were being encouraged to replace out of favour vines with premium varieties and vineyard acquisition or new plantings by the company itself would accentuate quality, he said.
